instances.label: Research-farm small-plot N trial: technician stakes out ~10 x 30 ft randomized, replicated plots, calibrates a plot spreader/backpack sprayer or hand-broadcasts, and applies assigned N rates, sources (urea, UAN, ESN, inhibitor-treated, manure) and timings (preplant, V6 sidedress into standing corn), keeping product off neighboring plots and buffer alleys and logging actual amounts; a minority of trials are field-length strips in a cooperator's field applied with production equipment on a prescription.

Georeferenced soil sampling of each plot for nitrate/ammonium: 6-12 cores per plot at 0-12 in (often also 12-24 in) at preplant, PSNT timing and post-harvest, composited per plot, bagged, labeled, chilled and delivered to the lab; done on wet, rutted or crop-covered ground and avoiding fertilizer bands and prior sample holes.

Loss-pathway monitoring in the trial: repeated N2O flux measurements from chamber collars in each treatment on a set schedule through the season, plus collection of nitrate leachate from suction lysimeters/tile-drain flow and runoff samples, with routine servicing of the field equipment.

In-season crop monitoring per plot: stand counts, growth staging, plant height, chlorophyll-meter/canopy greenness or NDVI readings on each plot at several dates through the season to relate crop N status to the fertilizer treatments.

Destructive plant sampling and harvest: ear-leaf or whole-plant tissue collection at V6 and silking, biomass cuts, then plot-by-plot grain harvest with a plot combine, recording per-plot weight and moisture and drawing a labeled grain subsample for N analysis without mixing material between plots.

Laboratory processing and analysis: dry, grind and sieve soil and plant samples, weigh subsamples, KCl-extract and filter soils, run nitrate/ammonium colorimetry on extracts and water samples, combustion total N on tissue/grain, run standards and QC checks, and record results against plot IDs.

tasks.label: Prepare laboratory samples for analysis, following proper protocols to ensure that they will be stored, prepared, and disposed of efficiently and effectively.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume commercial ag testing lab (soil/plant tissue): intake of barcoded bagged soil samples, drying, grinding/sieving, scooping and weighing subsamples into extraction cups or digestion tubes, batching with QC standards, holding samples about a week for retest, then discarding residue. Repetitive standardized protocols, thousands of samples in season.

Dairy/DHI or milk-payment testing lab: racks of preserved milk vials arrive from farms and haulers; technician tempers, mixes/homogenizes, checks vial ID and volume, loads analyzers, subsamples for bacteriology, then refrigerates residual samples and discards spent vials. High volume, one standard container format.

Feed, forage, grain or residue chemistry lab: weigh ground sample, add solvents/salts/internal standards, extract, centrifuge, filter, dilute into labeled autosampler vials, store extracts cold pending the instrument run, and segregate solvent/solid waste. Fixed validated methods, batches of tens to hundreds.

Plant-breeding/seed genotyping lab: leaf punches or seed chips arrayed into 96-well plates, DNA extracted with magnetic-bead chemistry, quantified and normalized, PCR/assay plates set up, plates sealed, barcoded and stored at -20 C; tips and lysis waste discarded. Highly standardized plate-format work.

Animal-science/veterinary research lab: blood, serum, milk, semen, rumen fluid or fecal samples arrive in tubes; technician centrifuges, decaps, aliquots into labeled daughter tubes/cryovials, logs and racks them in fridge or -80 freezer, retrieves for add-on tests, and autoclaves or bags biohazard waste.

University, USDA or seed-company research lab supporting a scientist's project: small, varied batches of heterogeneous material from field plots, greenhouses or barns (whole plants, insects, roots with soil, tissue for cryogrinding), with protocols that change from experiment to experiment: dissecting, subsampling, liquid-nitrogen grinding, slide or media preparation, labeling and freezer archiving, chemical/biohazard disposal.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In an ag research or service lab, weighing dry chemicals/reagents (salts, buffers, media components, standards) on an analytical or top-loading balance to make up extractants, solutions, or culture media; reagent bottles, weigh boats/flasks, tare-and-record on a bench shared with people.

Measuring liquid reagents, solvents, extractants and standards by pipette, dispenser or graduated cylinder for assays (soil extractions, tissue digests, ELISA/PCR reagent mixes); tens to hundreds of vessels per batch, volumetric accuracy required.

Weighing subsamples of heterogeneous material — ground plant tissue, dried soil, grain, forage — into crucibles, digestion tubes or vials to a target mass, recording exact weights for downstream analysis.

Weighing out feed ingredients, premixes and micro-ingredients for animal nutrition trial diets and for feed-quality lab assays, in a research feed prep room or mill lab; kilogram-to-gram scale, dusty ingredients, bagged/binned stock.

Measuring pesticide, fertilizer or nutrient stock concentrates to prepare treatment solutions/spray mixes for greenhouse and growth-chamber trials in a research-station prep room; PPE, viscous or hazardous concentrates, jugs and graduated vessels.

tasks.label: Perform tests on seeds to evaluate seed viability.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine warm germination test on a field-crop seed lot (corn, soybean, wheat, rice) in a commercial, company or state seed lab: draw a working sample, count 400 seeds in 4 replicates, plant in moistened rolled towels or between paper, label, incubate in a germinator 5-14 days, then evaluate seedlings as normal/abnormal/dead per AOSA rules, count, and record the germination percentage.

Quality-control germination and radicle-emergence/vigor tests on vegetable, flower or other small-seeded lots at a seed company lab: 100-400 seeds counted onto blotters, top-of-paper trays or pleated paper, incubated under set temperature/light regimes, counted at scheduled intervals, seedlings classified and results entered into the lot record.

Genebank or research-station viability monitoring and breeding-line screens: many small samples (25-100 seeds) of stored accessions or experimental lines set up in petri dishes or on paper with standard protocols, incubated, scored for germination over time, data logged for the scientist.

Tetrazolium quick viability test in the lab: imbibe seeds overnight, bisect or pierce each seed with a scalpel/needle under magnification, immerse in 1% TZ solution, incubate, then examine each seed's embryo staining pattern under a stereomicroscope and classify viable vs non-viable, 100 seeds per sample.

Stress and vigor tests requiring soil, sand or aging chambers (cold test, saturated cold, accelerated aging) and dormancy-breaking pretreatments (scarification, stratification, GA soak) for dormant, native or wild species: prepare medium, plant, hold under stress conditions, then transfer, grow out and evaluate emergence/seedlings.

Quick viability check performed outside the lab: rag-doll or paper-towel test set up in a farm shop, seed dealer office or field-station work room for a producer's own seed lot, or emergence trays sown in a greenhouse; technician sets it up, keeps it moist, unrolls and counts sprouts after about a week and reports a rough germination percentage.

tasks.label: Supervise pest or weed control operations, including locating and identifying pests or weeds, selecting chemicals and application methods, or scheduling application.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Weed scouting in row-crop fields or research farm plots (corn, soybean, cotton, vegetables): walking/driving transects, identifying weed species and growth stages, estimating densities, mapping problem areas, and setting the herbicide/timing recommendation passed to the applicator. Open field, variable terrain, weather and residue.

Insect and disease scouting in field, orchard or vineyard crops: inspecting whorls, leaf undersides and fruit, sweep-net and beat-sheet counts, checking pheromone/sticky traps, identifying pest species, life stages and beneficials against economic thresholds, then deciding whether and when to treat. Open field/orchard, found conditions.

IPM monitoring in a greenhouse, screenhouse or growth-chamber range at a research station or production facility: routine bench/row scouting, sticky-card counts, identifying thrips, aphids, whitefly, mites and mildew, and scheduling pesticide or biocontrol releases for trials or production blocks.

Directing the application operation itself: staging and mixing chemicals in the chemical shed, verifying label rates, REI and PPE, calibrating the plot or field sprayer and checking nozzles, briefing and overseeing the applicator or crew, checking wind/drift and buffers, flagging plots, posting notices and completing pesticide-use records.

Post-application follow-up: revisiting treated fields or plots days to weeks later, rating percent control and any crop injury, counting surviving weeds or pests, and deciding on retreatment or a change in program.

tasks.label: Devise cultural methods or environmental controls for plants for which guidelines are sketchy or nonexistent.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Nursery or botanic-garden technician works out a propagation protocol for an uncommon native, rare, or newly acquired ornamental species with no published guidance: decides seed pretreatment (scarification, stratification), cutting type and timing, rooting hormone concentration, substrate mix, and mist/humidity regime by reasoning from related taxa, collection notes, and prior experience, then writes the protocol up for the nursery.

Research greenhouse or growth-chamber technician specifies the environmental control regime for a novel accession, wild crop relative, or transgenic line that must be brought to flowering: photoperiod, light spectrum and DLI, day/night temperature, humidity, CO2, and fertigation schedule; the output is a chamber program and written growing schedule handed to the PI and the greenhouse staff.

Plant tissue-culture / micropropagation technician devises an in-vitro culture regime for a recalcitrant species lacking any published protocol: basal medium and hormone ratios, sterilant and explant choice, subculture interval, light quality, and acclimatization steps; deliverable is a written media formulation and culture schedule.

Field or controlled-environment technician devises cultural practices for a specialty or newly introduced crop in a region with no extension guidelines: planting date, spacing, trellising or pruning, cover/shade, irrigation and nutrition scheduling; documents the recommendation for the grower cooperator or research plan.

Troubleshooting variant: plants of poorly documented material are failing (poor establishment, physiological disorder, unexplained decline) and the technician must devise a revised cultural or environmental regime on the spot, then communicate the amended protocol to growers, the PI, or the greenhouse manager.

tasks.label: Conduct insect or plant disease surveys.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scouting commercial row-crop production fields (corn, soybean, wheat, cotton): walking transects or driving field edges, pulling and inspecting plants, turning leaves, sweep-net or beat-cloth counts, estimating pest density, defoliation and disease incidence/severity, and writing a field report with threshold calls. Weather, mud, weeds, variable terrain and field-to-field layout differences are taken as found.

Rating insect damage and disease severity plot-by-plot in research-station or seed-company breeding nurseries and replicated trials: uniform planted plots on a mapped grid, controlled access, standard rating scales (e.g., % leaf area diseased, lesion counts), data entered per plot ID.

Running insect trap networks: siting and hanging pheromone/delta/sticky/light traps in orchards, vineyards, field margins and regulatory survey sites, servicing lures and liners on a route, then identifying and counting catch and reporting degree-day/threshold status.

Scouting a greenhouse, nursery or other controlled-environment facility: walking rows/benches, inspecting foliage and growing points for thrips, aphids, whitefly, mites and powdery mildew/botrytis, reading yellow sticky cards, and mapping hot spots for the IPM record.

Collecting symptomatic plant material for a disease survey: locating affected plants, excising leaf/stem/root tissue, bagging and labeling with GPS and metadata, transporting, then confirming the pathogen by microscopy, ELISA or PCR in the lab and recording the survey result.

tasks.label: Perform general nursery duties, such as propagating standard varieties of plant materials, collecting and germinating seeds, maintaining cuttings of plants, or controlling environmental conditions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Propagating standard varieties by cuttings in a research/production propagation house: taking shoot cuttings from stock plants, trimming to node, dipping in rooting hormone, sticking hundreds to thousands of cuttings into media-filled flats, labeling by variety, and placing under mist. Greenhouse/headhouse setting, institution-controlled.

Seed work: counting out seed lots by accession/variety, sowing into plug trays, pots or germination substrate (paper/blotter, dishes), setting them in a germination chamber or greenhouse, then scoring emergence/germination and recording counts. Headhouse and seed-lab setting.

Potting up and transplanting: moving rooted cuttings, plugs and seedlings into larger containers with fresh media, firming, labeling, and watering in — done in the headhouse/potting area of a greenhouse or nursery.

Moving, spacing and consolidating container plants and trays: distributing pots onto beds/benches, re-spacing as plants grow, collecting and staging material between propagation house, greenhouse benches and outdoor nursery pads. Institution-controlled greenhouse and nursery yard.

Controlling environmental conditions: setting and adjusting temperature, humidity, light/photoperiod, CO2, mist intervals and irrigation/fertigation (EC, pH) in greenhouse compartments and growth chambers; checking sensors, logging conditions, responding to alarms and out-of-range readings.

Outdoor collection of propagation material: walking stock beds and field plots to collect mature seed heads/pods by accession into labeled bags, cutting scion/hardwood cuttings from selected plants, and hand tending (roguing, weeding, pruning stock plants) in variable weather and terrain.

tasks.label: Record environmental data from field samples of soil, air, water, or pests to monitor the effectiveness of integrated pest management (IPM) practices.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Row-crop IPM scouting round (corn, soybean, cotton, vegetables): technician walks assigned transects/plots in a grower or research field, visually inspects plants and checks pheromone/sticky traps, counts insects, eggs and feeding damage, and logs counts, growth stage and conditions by GPS point in a scouting app/spreadsheet to track whether the IPM program is holding pests below threshold.

Active/destructive field sampling for pest counts: sweep-net sets in soybean/alfalfa, beat-sheet or shake samples, dissecting stalks/fruit, digging roots for rootworm injury ratings, washing or sorting captured specimens in a pan, then tallying species and recording numbers per plot. Requires handling plants and specimens, not just viewing them.

Perennial/specialty crop monitoring (apple, almond, grape, citrus): making rounds of pheromone/camera traps hung in the canopy, counting moths, rating disease severity and mite/scale presence on sampled leaves, and downloading weather-station/degree-day data, all logged into the block's IPM record.

Greenhouse/nursery IPM monitoring: walking benches or rows on a fixed weekly route, reading yellow/blue sticky cards, inspecting leaves for thrips, whitefly, aphids and spider mites, checking biocontrol establishment, and recording counts per zone in the facility's monitoring log.

Field soil sampling tied to pest/soil monitoring: pulling georeferenced soil cores from monitored plots (nematode/soil-insect assays, soil condition), taking in-situ probe readings (moisture, temperature, pH/EC), bagging and labeling samples, and recording location, depth and reading data for the trial or field record.

Laboratory leg of the work: logging in received soil/water/insect samples, drying, weighing, sieving/extracting, running analyses on bench instruments (or counting specimens under a scope), transcribing or exporting results into a LIMS/spreadsheet, and running QC checks before the data are reported.

sources.claim: Solinftec's Solix is a solar-powered autonomous ground robot operating on US commercial farms that continuously monitors crops and records field-level intelligence including pest presence, weed density, plant emergence and growth stage; over 100 robots deployed in the US as of March 2026.
sources.transferJustification: The robot's continuous field monitoring output (pest presence, weed density, stand, growth stage, geo-referenced and time-stamped in the grower platform) is the same class of field pest/crop record the technician compiles on a scouting round.

sources.title: Solinftec Announces Successful First Commercial Season of Solix Sprayer Robot - CropLife
sources.claim: Solix robots completed a first full commercial season in Midwest fields and report, per pass, insect identification and thresholds, disease identification and thresholds, weed densities and crop populations to the grower platform.
sources.transferJustification: Insect/disease identification and threshold reporting from a field pass is the data-recording output that IPM effectiveness monitoring consumes.

sources.title: The Three Key Benefits of Drone Scouting - Taranis
sources.claim: Taranis' commercial drone scouting service flies pre-planned missions over row-crop fields and outputs leaf-level insect identification and field-wide severity, delivered as insect-pressure, disease and stand-count records in an advisor dashboard.
sources.transferJustification: Same output as a scouting record (species-level insect pressure per field); cited only as supporting context because on-site pilot involvement means autonomy is not established.

sources.claim: An autonomous robotic system (Agrobot Lala) performs in-field soil sampling, on-board sample preparation and nitrate analysis at AI-selected field locations and uploads results to a cloud platform, demonstrating automated in-situ soil measurement and data recording.

tasks.label: Determine the germination rates of seeds planted in specified areas.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Row-crop research/production field: technician walks corn, soybean, cotton or sunflower plots ~2-3 weeks after planting, counts emerged seedlings over measured lengths of row (or whole small plots), and computes percent emergence against the known seeding rate; outdoor conditions, mud, weeds, variable stands.

Drilled or broadcast dense stands in the field (wheat, barley, canola, forage grasses, turf, cover-crop mixes): technician throws quadrats or measures row lengths, kneels and counts small overlapping seedlings per unit area, and converts to establishment/germination percent.

Greenhouse, nursery or growth-chamber trials: seeds sown in plug trays or soil flats on benches; technician counts emerged seedlings per tray/cell over several days, records germination percent per lot, variety or treatment, and flags usable plant counts per batch.

Seed-testing laboratory standard germination test (AOSA/ISTA): 4 x 100 seeds of a lot placed on moist paper (top-of-paper, between-paper or rolled towel), incubated in a germinator at a prescribed regime, then evaluated at first and final count, classifying normal seedlings, abnormals, hard and dead seed, and reporting percent germination.

Laboratory petri-dish/blotter germination of small-seeded research species (Arabidopsis, lettuce, vegetable or grass seed) in a growth room: dozens of plates scored repeatedly for radicle emergence, germination curves and final percentages, often under a stereomicroscope.

Laboratory tests on dormancy-prone or specialty seed (native forbs, tree and shrub seed, weed-science studies): stratification pretreatments, irregular seed coats, ungerminated seeds pressed or cut open and follow-up tetrazolium staining to separate viable from dead seed before reporting a germination/viability figure.

sources.transferJustification: Stand/emergence counting in planted plots is exactly the numerator of a field germination-rate determination; the paper explicitly frames emergence rate and stand counting as the manual traits being replaced.

sources.developer: EarthSense Inc. with Corteva Agriscience and UIUC

sources.transferJustification: Traits reported here are LAI, height, stem width and ear height rather than stand count; cited to establish that this robot operates routinely and at scale, unattended, in the same breeding-plot field environment where emergence counts are taken.

tasks.label: Transplant trees, vegetables, or horticultural plants.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Research greenhouse or headhouse: technician pricks out germinated seedlings/plugs from seed or plug trays and transplants them into pots or larger cell trays for a trial; uniform young plants, batches of hundreds to a few thousand, each pot tagged with an entry/treatment code; bench-and-aisle layout, standard media and containers.

Greenhouse, growth chamber, or hydroponic bay: potting up established plants into larger containers or setting them into ground beds/hydroponic modules; larger root balls, tangled roots and foliage, some root washing or trimming, careful handling of individual research plants, labels transferred with the plant.

Experiment-station field: transplanting vegetable or horticultural seedlings into prepared beds according to a plot map, with a different entry/genotype in each small plot, plot markers and flags, hand setting or a carousel transplanter with a riding crew; soil, wind and moisture conditions as they come that day.

Experiment-station or cooperator field: bulk, uniform transplanting of a single variety over a large prepared, bedded block (seed increase, large uniform trial, production-scale demonstration) using standard field transplanting practice, continuous rows at fixed spacing with water applied at planting.

Tissue-culture lab / propagation room: transferring in vitro plantlets out of flasks or vessels and transplanting them into plugs or acclimatization trays (ex vitro transfer), plus micro-transplanting of small delicate plantlets under a laminar-flow hood; sterile technique, very delicate stems and roots.

Outdoor woody-plant transplanting: setting tree seedlings, liners, or grafted rootstocks into an orchard, vineyard, nursery field row, or forest/plantation research site; digging or auguring holes, uneven ground, residue and stones, root-ball or bare-root handling, hand firming and watering.

sources.title: Less labor required with automated sticking (FloralDaily)
sources.claim: Visser's AutoStix is a commercially sold greenhouse machine that automatically plants cuttings held in strips into plugs, pots or trays at 10,000-11,000 cuttings/hour on an inline conveyor.
sources.transferJustification: Sticking cuttings is the same physical transplanting act as setting a seedling: a propagule is gripped and inserted to depth into media in a plug, pot or tray, at comparable size and delicacy.

tasks.label: Prepare culture media, following standard procedures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Microbiological plate media in an agricultural research/plant-pathology or food/soil microbiology lab: weigh dehydrated powder (PDA, nutrient agar, selective agars), dissolve 1–5 L in DI water, autoclave, cool to ~50 °C, pour 50–300 Petri dishes in a laminar-flow hood, label, dry and store.

Plant tissue-culture medium in a micropropagation/transformation lab: dissolve MS salts, sucrose, vitamins, adjust pH to ~5.7 with NaOH/HCl, add agar or Gelrite, dispense measured volumes into culture tubes, Magenta boxes or jars, cap and autoclave the filled vessels, cool flat or slanted.

Media requiring heat-labile or biological additives: after sterilization and cooling, aseptically add filter-sterilized antibiotics, plant growth regulators, blood or serum (or filter-sterilize the whole medium through 0.22 µm), mix and dispense; recipes vary experiment to experiment in small custom batches.

Broths, dilution blanks and animal-nutrition/rumen culture media: dispense measured volumes into tubes, flasks or bottles, cap loosely, autoclave, sometimes gas with CO2 or prepare pre-reduced anaerobic medium, then cool and store.

Insect or nematode rearing diet ('media') in an insectary diet kitchen: mix and cook agar-based artificial diet, dispense hot diet into rearing cups, trays or tubes, allow to gel, cover and hold for use.

Small batch prepared at a field station, farm lab or greenhouse headhouse bench: improvised equipment and variable layout, a few hundred mL of medium made up, sterilized in a small autoclave or pressure cooker, and poured into whatever vessels are on hand.

sources.date: 2023 (product line in commercial sale; page current 2026)
sources.title: Automating media preparation and dispensing in microbiology laboratories
sources.claim: INTEGRA's MEDIACLAVE media sterilizer, which dissolves, stirs and sterilizes 1–30 L of culture medium in one vessel, links directly to the MEDIAJET Petri dish filler ... give a hands-free run from bulk medium to finished poured plates (~900 plates/hour).

sources.system: Automated media sterilisers and plate pourers/fillers (class of instruments)
sources.title: Automated Laboratory Media Preparation - rapidmicrobiology
sources.claim: Commercial fully automated media sterilizers and pourers/fillers run walk-away: dehydrated media is loaded into the machine, a program is selected, and finished poured plates or filled tubes come out with controlled sterilization and pouring temperatures.

sources.title: APS ONE™ automated culture media plate pouring system | bioMérieux
sources.claim: bioMérieux's APS ONE automated pourer-stacker fills and stacks hundreds of Petri dishes per hour of in-house prepared media, and its MASTERCLAVE preparators prepare and sterilize up to 60 L of broth or agar, forming a commercial media-preparation chain used in food and agricultural testing labs.

sources.system: Automated culture media preparation and dispenser systems (MASTERCLAVE, MEDIACLAVE class)
sources.title: Automated Culture Media Preparation and Dispenser System — Microbe Online
sources.claim: Automated media preparators dissolve powder with a powerful stirrer and sterilize in the same vessel so no operator transfer to an autoclave is needed, but the powder weighing and water measuring steps are still done by hand by the technician.

sources.system: METTLER TOLEDO Quantos automated powder/liquid dosing system

sources.claim: METTLER TOLEDO's Quantos automated dosing system gravimetrically dispenses solids and liquids to prepare samples at a target concentration without an operator weighing by hand; the same unit, with cartridge hotels holding up to 20 different solids, was operated by the Liverpool mobile robot.
sources.transferJustification: Weighing dehydrated media powder to a target mass and adding a measured volume of water is the first step of culture-media preparation; the objects (free-flowing powders, aqueous liquids) and the gravimetric precision required are the same.

sources.title: A mobile robotic chemist | Nature
sources.claim: The Liverpool mobile robotic chemist, a free-roaming KUKA mobile manipulator, autonomously ran 688 formulation experiments over eight days in a wet chemistry lab that was otherwise unmodified, dosing solids at a Quantos cartridge station, dispensing liquids, capping vials and operating instruments.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: preparing multi-component liquid formulations from weighed powders and dispensed liquids in a human lab. It shows autonomous weighing/dissolving in an unmodified lab, but the demonstration contains no sterilization, pH adjustment or aseptic dispensing, so it does not substantiate whole-instance media preparation.

sources.developer: Robotic Biology Institute / RIKEN / AIST (Kanda et al.)
sources.title: Cell Culture: Implementing robotics and artificial intelligence | eLife
sources.claim: The LabDroid Maholo dual-arm robot performed complex manual cell-culture procedures, including scheduled medium exchange and dispensing of sterile media into culture plates, inside its enclosed purpose-built cell-processing station.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: aseptic handling and dispensing of sterile liquid media and supplements into culture vessels. Same objects (sterile media, pipettes, culture vessels), same aseptic requirement, inside an enclosed robot-built station, which is the aseptic-addition step of media preparation.

sources.system: Mass-rearing diet preparation and dispensing machinery
sources.developer: IAEA/FAO SIT programmes and rearing-facility suppliers
sources.title: Mass-Rearing for the Sterile Insect Technique (review chapter)
sources.claim: Insect mass-rearing facilities for the sterile insect technique use described automated systems for nearly all production stages, including artificial-diet preparation and dispensing into rearing containers.
sources.transferJustification: Insect artificial diet is a cooked, gelled rearing medium; mixing, heating and dispensing it into rearing cups is operationally the same as cooking agar medium and pouring it into vessels.

tasks.label: Respond to general inquiries or requests from the public.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Prepare or present agricultural demonstrations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Establish and maintain result-demonstration plots at a university research farm or extension demonstration center ahead of a field day: stake the layout, plant treatment strips with plot equipment, apply the treatments being compared, install plot signs/flags, mow alleys and keep the site presentable through the season.

Set up demonstration strips or a method-comparison trial on a cooperating grower's field or other as-found outdoor site: work around the farmer's existing crop, terrain, and equipment, place roadside/edge-of-field signage, and keep the demo identifiable and safe for visitors.

Present a tour stop at a field day or twilight tour: lead 20-50 growers into the plots, dig or pull plants, split stalks, show insect or disease damage and yield differences, explain treatments and data, and field unscripted technical questions in wind, heat, or mud.

Run a hands-on method demonstration inside a controlled facility (barn, greenhouse, teaching lab, shop, or expo hall): e.g., sprayer/spreader calibration, soil or forage sampling, grafting, seed germination testing, livestock handling or body-condition scoring, with participants watching and then trying it themselves.

Prepare and staff an indoor exhibit or tabletop demonstration for school groups, 4-H, or a commodity trade show: assemble specimens, soil/plant samples, working models and posters, set up and man the table, and explain the material to a stream of visitors.

sources.title: LaserWeeder — Carbon Robotics
sources.claim: Autonomous laser weeding machines are commercially owned and operated by growers in production fields, showing that autonomous field operations exist for single, well-defined agronomic sub-steps (weed control) but not for laying out, planting, labeling and maintaining a multi-treatment demonstration plot.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous in-field crop care. It shares the outdoor cropland environment of demonstration-plot upkeep, but covers only one operation on a uniform field; it does not establish differentiated treatment strips, install interpretive signage, or bring a site to a presentation standard, so it does not substantiate completing the demonstration-preparation instances.

sources.system: Autonomous 9RX tractor with second-generation autonomy kit
sources.title: John Deere Reveals New Autonomous Machines & Technology at CES 2025
sources.claim: Row-crop tractor autonomy is limited to whole-field single operations such as tillage and orchard spraying with an operator supervising remotely; no cited system plans and installs a labeled multi-treatment demonstration plot.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous tillage of a production field. Same outdoor cropland setting, but the operation is uniform across a field and is announced/limited-release rather than performing plot-scale treatment layout, signage, and season-long presentation upkeep, so capability does not carry over to preparing agricultural demonstrations.

sources.system: 5G-enabled tour guide robot (5G-TOURS project); earlier RHINO/Deutsches Museum Bonn tour-guide robot
sources.developer: 5G-TOURS EU consortium; Carnegie Mellon University / University of Bonn (RHINO)
sources.title: Tour guide robot: a 5G-enabled robot museum guide (Frontiers in Robotics and AI)
sources.claim: Autonomous guide robots have been deployed in museums to navigate to exhibits and deliver prepared explanations to visitors, but they only narrate scripted content and do not manipulate specimens or equipment or answer unscripted technical questions.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomously guiding and informing an audience inside a structured facility. It is the closest 'presenting' capability found, but it delivers fixed narration along a known route with no handling of plants, samples, or equipment and no expert Q&A, so it does not substantiate presenting an agricultural demonstration.

tasks.label: Assess comparative soil erosion from various planting or tillage systems, such as conservation tillage with mulch or ridge till systems, no-till systems, or conventional tillage systems with or without moldboard plows.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Residue-cover assessment on replicated tillage treatment plots at a university/USDA research farm after planting: walk each plot, run line-point transects (or photo-grid), record percent cover for no-till, mulch-till, ridge-till and moldboard-plow treatments, and tabulate treatment means. Plots are surveyed, staked and institution-controlled; ground is muddy/uneven with standing stubble.

On-farm comparative assessment across cooperating producers' fields (no-till vs. conventional): travel to each field, run residue transects, walk the slope to locate and measure rills and ephemeral gullies, photograph and GPS-tag erosion features, and note crop, slope and recent storms. Layout, access, terrain and obstacles differ site to site.

Storm-event servicing of instrumented erosion/runoff plots at a research station: after each runoff event, drive to the plots, read flumes/tipping buckets and dataloggers, retrieve flow-weighted runoff samples from automatic samplers or measure sediment in collection tanks/Coshocton splitters, rinse and reset intakes, and log volumes per tillage treatment.

Rainfall-simulator campaign on paired tillage plots: install plot frames/borders, set up and calibrate the portable simulator, apply a controlled storm, collect timed runoff aliquots, record time-to-runoff and infiltration, and compute comparative runoff and soil-loss rates for each tillage system.

Georeferenced soil core sampling across tillage treatment blocks at the research farm: pull cores at prescribed grid points and set depth increments, bag, label and barcode them for lab analysis of erosion-related indicators (organic carbon, texture, stratification) across treatments.

Laboratory processing of the sediment and soil samples and compilation of comparative soil-loss data: filter/settle and oven-dry sediment, weigh, sieve and grind soils, run aggregate-stability and bulk-density determinations, enter weights into spreadsheets/RUSLE2-WEPP inputs and produce treatment comparisons. Ordinary shared soils lab with ovens, balances, sieve shakers and fume hoods.

sources.system: DJI Matrice 300 / Zenmuse L1 UAS with K-means and PCA-Otsu crop residue cover estimation
sources.developer: Purdue University (Jung et al.), published in Remote Sensing (MDPI)
sources.title: Automated Crop Residue Estimation via Unsupervised Techniques Using High-Resolution UAS RGB Imagery
sources.claim: Autonomous UAS imagery with unsupervised image analysis estimates crop residue cover in corn and soybean fields across no-till and conventionally tilled fields, validated against line-point transect ground truth (K-means R2 = 0.79); flights used a DJI Matrice 300 mapping platform.
sources.transferJustification: Same measurement the technician makes when comparing tillage systems: percent crop residue cover per field/plot, validated against the line-point transect method the worker uses, and reported separately for no-till versus conventionally tilled fields.

instances.label: Grid or management-zone soil sampling of row-crop fields (corn/soybean/wheat): driving an ATV/UTV or truck with a hydraulic probe to GPS-referenced points, pulling cores at a specified depth through residue, compositing, bagging, barcoding/labeling and geo-logging each sample on a field data recorder, then shipping to the lab. Done in spring or post-harvest fall, in stubble, mud, ruts and cold.

In-season georeferenced scouting/attribute collection: traversing the field on foot or by UTV, recording geotagged stand counts, growth stage, weed/insect/disease pressure, stress patterns and photos into a rugged field data recorder/GIS app for later mapping.

Aerial data collection over fields: flying an RTK-capable mapping/multispectral drone on a planned mission to capture georeferenced imagery and elevation for field boundaries, waterways, drainage and crop-health layers, then exporting to GIS/FMIS.

Yield-data system work off the field: installing/verifying mass-flow, moisture and header sensors on customer combines, running calibration loads at several flow rates in the shop/field yard, then retrieving cards or telematics files and cleaning/QC-ing the yield dataset.

Capturing georeferenced yield data during the harvest pass itself: the machine traverses the standing crop while the monitor logs mass flow, moisture and position, producing a complete yield map for the field.

On-the-go soil/field attribute mapping: towing an EC/gamma/elevation sensor cart behind a UTV or tractor on parallel swaths across the field at set spacing, logging continuous georeferenced sensor data for zone maps.

tasks.label: Install, calibrate, or maintain sensors, mechanical controls, GPS-based vehicle guidance systems, or computer settings.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retrofit install of a precision hardware kit on a customer's machine at the farm shop/yard or dealer bay: mount GNSS receiver bracket on a tractor/sprayer/combine cab, route and secure a wiring harness through the cab, mount display and controller, tap CAN/ISOBUS and power, install steering motor or plumb a hydraulic steering valve, then road/field validate. Machine makes, models and ages vary widely; brackets sometimes drilled or fabricated on the spot.

Seasonal calibration of machine-mounted sensors and controls: combine yield-monitor mass-flow and moisture calibration across grain flow rates with weigh-wagon references, planter seed meter/seed-tube and downforce sensor calibration, sprayer flow meter, pressure and speed-sensor calibration with catch tests, auto-steer steering-sensor and implement-geometry calibration. Done with the machine running in the field or farmyard, in dust and grain, under time pressure.

Install and maintain fixed field sensing infrastructure: site and auger in soil moisture probes with good soil contact, erect and wire a weather station or RTK base station mast with solar panel and battery, seal enclosures, install pivot/VRI control panel sensors, then return seasonally to clean, re-level, replace batteries, and repair rodent- or weather-damaged wiring. Open fields, mud, wind, no fixed layout.

Set up and update controller/display software and settings: load machine and implement profiles, enter offsets and geometry, select correction source and configure base station/RTK network settings, apply firmware and software updates by USB or over the air, enter unlock codes, configure data transfer and field boundaries. Performed in the cab at the customer's farm, in the shop office, or remotely.

In-season troubleshooting and repair of a failed sensor or mechanical control: diagnose an erratic seed sensor, plugged optical sensor, corroded harness pin, failed flow meter or a sticking variable-rate drive linkage/hydraulic valve; disassemble, clean or replace the part, reconnect, and verify operation. Usually at the field edge or in the customer's shop, under downtime pressure.

tasks.label: Identify spatial coordinates, using remote sensing and Global Positioning System (GPS) data.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: At a desk in an ag-retail or co-op office, the technician georeferences drone or satellite imagery of a client's field and extracts the latitude/longitude of features seen in the imagery (weed patches, drowned-out spots, standing water, stand gaps) so the coordinates can be handed to a scout or a variable-rate prescription.

In GIS software, the technician converts raw GNSS/RTK logs from field data recorders, sprayers, or combines into clean coordinate sets "jumps", drift, and datum/projection mismatches are corrected, and field boundary vertices and headland coordinates are established for the farm record.

The technician determines the coordinate list for a grid or zone soil-sampling plan by overlaying imagery-derived management zones on the boundary layer and outputting a georeferenced point file (shapefile/GPX/ISOXML) loaded onto the sampler's handheld or rover.

Working from a client phone call or agronomist note, the technician pinpoints the coordinates of a specific in-field location (a pivot point, tile line intersection, sensor or trap station, damaged area for an insurance/agronomy report) by cross-referencing imagery, prior GPS records, and public parcel/CLU layers.

In the field or shop, the technician verifies coordinate accuracy by comparing a handheld/RTK rover reading at a known point against imagery- or map-derived coordinates, and resolves offsets (base station position, correction service, datum epoch) before the coordinates are published to the machinery fleet.

In-field demonstration of a variable-rate chemical/fertilizer applicator: technician loads a prescription map into the rate controller, calibrates the machine, runs a strip across a demo plot while observers ride along or watch from the headland, then pulls up the as-applied map and explains where and why rates changed.

Office, farm-shop, or extension-classroom demonstration of GIS and computer mapping software: walking a grower, agronomist, or class through yield maps, soil-sample layers, satellite/drone imagery, and building a variable-rate prescription on a laptop or projector, fielding questions throughout.

Trade show, dealer open house, or field-day booth: repeated short demonstrations of guidance displays, receivers, simulators, drones, and mapping software to a stream of visitors, including hands-on trials, in an exhibit hall or on a demonstration plot.

Demonstration of survey/mapping data-collection equipment on a customer's farm: setting up an RTK base and rover, walking or driving field boundaries, tile lines, and elevation points, or flying a mapping drone mission over a field, then showing the resulting map/data product to the farm staff and explaining its use.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Data-collection campaign for a weed-identification model: flying automated drone missions or driving a camera/sensor rig over commercial row-crop fields at multiple growth stages, times of day and weather conditions, capturing georeferenced imagery and uploading organized datasets for the development team.

Routine in-field ground-truthing for model validation: covering trial fields to record which common weed species are present, their density and growth stage, georeferencing the observations, and delivering a reference map that the developers compare against algorithm output.

Edge-case ground-truthing: locating unfamiliar, damaged, or look-alike vegetation that the detector misclassified, digging or clipping specimens, keying out or bagging them for lab/herbarium confirmation, and reconciling the confirmed identity with the model's error cases.

In-field validation runs of a spot-spray / smart-sprayer system: running the machine over designated test acres and check strips, monitoring detection and nozzle actuation, and logging application performance, herbicide savings and missed weeds for the developers.

Prototype and beta hardware work in the farm shop and on the machine: fabricating brackets, mounting cameras, sensor booms and controllers on a sprayer or tractor, routing and terminating wiring harnesses, powering up, configuring, and troubleshooting faults on one-off pre-release kits.

Controlled testing indoors: bench characterization of nozzles and sensing hardware (spray pattern/patternator runs, droplet size, valve latency) on a lab rig, and greenhouse or growth-room trials with planted weed and crop targets imaged and treated under set conditions and scored over time.

roles.description: Work with food scientists or technologists to perform standardized qualitative and quantitative tests to determine physical or chemical properties of food or beverage products. Includes technicians who assist in research and development of production technology, quality control, packaging, processing, and use of foods.

tasks.label: Taste or smell foods or beverages to ensure that flavors meet specifications or to select samples with specific characteristics.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine in-plant QC conformity check: technician pulls in-process or finished product samples (soft drink, juice, milk, sauce, snack) in the plant QC lab, tastes/smells each against the approved gold standard, and records pass/fail or a score for batch release. High volume, familiar products, known reference standard.

Serving on a trained descriptive or difference panel in a sensory booth lab: coded samples served under controlled conditions; technician rates 15-30 attributes (aroma, taste, mouthfeel, aftertaste) on scales or performs triangle/duo-trio discrimination and submits a ballot pooled with other panelists.

Shelf-life / stability study: technician tastes and smells samples of the same product held at ambient and accelerated conditions at set time points, looking for developing off-flavors (rancid, cardboard, stale, light-struck) and judging whether the product is still within spec.

R&D bench tasting of prototypes: technician tastes novel formulations, reformulations and competitor products in the pilot plant/R&D lab, describes off-notes verbally and gives developers open-ended direction (too sweet, metallic aftertaste, ingredient swap detectable), often on one-off products with no reference model.

Incoming raw material / ingredient sensory acceptance at the QC lab or receiving dock: sniffing oils for rancidity, checking a flavor concentrate, spice, cocoa or dairy ingredient lot against the retained standard, and accepting or rejecting the delivery.

Selecting samples or lots with specified sensory characteristics: e.g., picking the sweetest fruit lots or batches with a target aroma intensity out of many candidates for further testing, blending or panel work, in a QC lab, packhouse or warehouse.

instances.label: Production-floor CCP checks in a food plant: technician walks the line on a set schedule, pulls product at cook exit, chiller exit and filler, inserts a calibrated probe (or takes an IR screening read), waits for stabilization, records on the HACCP log, and calls for a setpoint change or product hold when a reading is out of spec.

Continuous thermal-process monitoring and control: technician watches in-line product temperature readouts and charts on a pasteurizer, retort, cook oven or chiller, adjusts setpoints or diverts/holds product to keep it inside the validated time-temperature schedule, and verifies the recording chart/electronic record for the run.

Storage rounds inside the plant: technician makes scheduled rounds of coolers, freezers, tempering and warm rooms, reads and logs each room's temperature display/chart, checks for out-of-range or defrost conditions, and alerts refrigeration/maintenance or adjusts the setpoint.

Receiving/shipping verification at the dock: technician meets an inbound refrigerated load, opens cases and takes pulp/core temperatures of several product units, compares to spec and carrier records, and documents accept, hold or reject.

QC lab work: technician sets, verifies and records temperatures of water baths, incubators, ovens, and refrigerated/frozen retain and sample storage; holds samples and test media at required temperatures through an assay; documents and corrects out-of-range conditions.

Pilot-plant / R&D thermal trials: technician instruments product with thermocouples or wireless data loggers, runs a cook-chill, pasteurization or retort trial, monitors the product temperature curve in real time, adjusts process parameters to hit the target profile, and reports the lethality/temperature data.

Preventive maintenance on analytical instruments: HPLC/GC column, septum, inlet liner, filter, seal and detector-lamp changes; purging and flushing lines; cleaning flow cells and syringes; then running check standards/system-suitability to confirm the instrument is back in spec. Also texture-analyzer probe swaps and viscometer spindle cleaning.

Cleaning and sanitizing pilot-plant/processing equipment used in product development: circulating detergent and sanitizer through tanks, homogenizer, pasteurizer and fill lines, rinsing, and verifying cleanliness by swab or rinse-water test before the next trial run.

Scheduled inspection/condition-monitoring round of lab and pilot-plant equipment: walking the area, checking for leaks, unusual noise, overheating or wear, reading gauges and freezer/incubator/water-bath temperature displays against limits, and logging findings or raising a service ticket.

Daily/weekly sanitation of lab surfaces and equipment exteriors: wiping down benches, biosafety cabinet and fume hood interiors, balance tables, sample prep areas and cold-room shelving with disinfectant on a fixed schedule.

tasks.label: Examine chemical or biological samples to identify cell structures or to locate bacteria or extraneous material, using a microscope.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Food/beverage plant or contract QC micro lab: technician prepares and examines stained smears (Gram stain) or wet mounts from enrichments, cultures or product, at 100x-1000x, to detect and morphologically identify bacteria, yeasts and molds; records findings on the lot record.

Brewery, dairy-culture or fermentation lab: technician loads a hemocytometer or counting chamber with a diluted yeast/starter-culture slurry, stains (methylene blue/AO-PI), counts cells and dead cells under the microscope, and reports concentration and viability for pitching decisions.

Microanalytical/filth bench: technician scans filter papers, sieved residues or mounts from a light-filth extraction under a stereomicroscope and compound scope to find and taxonomically identify insect fragments, rodent hairs, mites, feather barbules, and to identify unknown foreign bodies from consumer complaints against FDA defect action levels.

Routine standardized structural counts on a fixed product matrix: e.g., Howard mold-count of tomato products, counting fat/ice crystals or emulsion droplets, or particle/cell counts in a defined slide preparation, repeated many times per shift on the same matrix.

Ad hoc R&D/authenticity microscopy: examining stained sections or mounts of varied and novel food matrices (starch granules, plant tissue, muscle fiber, spice powders) to identify cell structures, verify ingredient identity or detect adulteration, judging morphology against reference material.

High-volume raw-milk/liquid product testing lab: examining milk samples for somatic cells and for bacteria (direct microscopic count / individual bacteria count) to grade hygienic quality, hundreds of samples per shift.

tasks.label: Conduct standardized tests on food, beverages, additives, or preservatives to ensure compliance with standards and regulations regarding factors such as color, texture, or nutrients.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine physicochemical bench QC in a plant or contract lab: technician receives incoming-ingredient and finished-product samples (bottles, jars, pouches), opens/mixes them, and runs standard tests — pH, titratable acidity, Brix/density, moisture (Karl Fischer or oven), water activity — against spec sheets, logging results into LIMS.

Instrumental color and texture testing: technician prepares specimens (cuts, levels, tempers to standard temperature), measures color with a spectrophotometer/colorimeter against L*a*b* tolerances, and runs texture-analyzer tests (compression, penetration, shear) on products such as baked goods, cheese, meat, or confectionery.

Nutrient/compositional analysis in an analytical lab: grind/homogenize sample, weigh subsamples, run protein (Kjeldahl/Dumas), fat (extraction), ash, fiber, moisture, or additive/preservative content by HPLC/GC/ICP/FTIR for nutrition-label and regulatory compliance, including standards, blanks and QC checks.

Microbiological compliance testing: weigh and homogenize sample with diluent, prepare serial dilutions, plate or fill enumeration devices for total count, coliforms, Enterobacteriaceae, yeast/mold, incubate, and enumerate against regulatory/customer limits.

Sensory/organoleptic evaluation: technician prepares coded samples and personally scores appearance, aroma, taste, mouthfeel against reference standards or serves as a trained panelist in a standardized difference/descriptive test to clear a batch for release.

Line-side/at-line conformance checks in the production plant: technician pulls product from the running line on a schedule and performs standardized checks on color, appearance/defects and product uniformity, recording conformance and flagging out-of-spec product to operators.

tasks.label: Train newly hired laboratory personnel.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench-side orientation of a newly hired QC technician in a food plant or R&D lab: the experienced technician walks the new hire through sample receipt, prep, and routine assays (pH, titratable acidity, moisture, Brix), explaining each SOP step, watching the trainee attempt it, and correcting technique verbally.

Instrument-specific training and competency sign-off: showing a new hire how to calibrate and run a specific instrument (moisture/texture analyzer, HPLC, viscometer, colorimeter), explaining acceptance criteria and troubleshooting, then observing the trainee run duplicate samples and documenting proficiency on a competency checklist.

Classroom/desk-based training on documentation and compliance: GMP, HACCP/food safety plan, allergen and sanitation procedures, chemical hygiene and PPE rules, LIMS/spreadsheet data entry, and record-keeping conventions, delivered one-on-one or in a small group with slides, SOP binders, or e-learning modules.

Ongoing coaching during the trainee's first weeks: answering questions on shift, reviewing the trainee's results and worksheets for errors, re-explaining technique after out-of-spec or inconsistent results, and gradually releasing the trainee to work independently.

Group training session for several new hires or cross-trained staff on a newly validated method, a revised SOP, or a customer/audit requirement, including a demonstration run and a written or practical check of understanding.

tasks.label: Provide assistance to food scientists or technologists in research and development, production technology, or quality control.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Quality-control analytical bench work in a plant or contract food lab: technician receives incoming line/ingredient/finished-product samples, weighs and preps them (extraction, dilution, filtration), runs standardized physical/chemical tests (pH, moisture, fat, Brix, residues/contaminants by LC-MS/GC), and enters results into LIMS for the food scientist, flagging out-of-spec results.

R&D bench support in a product-development lab/pilot kitchen: per the scientist's protocol, gravimetrically weighs and doses ingredients, mixes/emulsifies/heats bench-scale formulation variants, labels and stores prototypes, and measures basic properties (viscosity, pH, color, texture) for the scientist's design matrix.

Food microbiology / food-safety lab support: prepares and pours media, weighs and homogenizes food portions, performs serial dilutions and plating (pour/spread/spiral), loads incubators, counts colonies, runs rapid pathogen assays and environmental swabs, records counts.

Pilot-plant and production-technology support on the plant floor: helps set up and change over pilot/production equipment (extruder, mixer, filler, retort, dryer), charges ingredients, runs the trial with the scientist, pulls timed in-process samples from lines and vessels, records process parameters, and breaks down and cleans equipment afterward.

Sensory and shelf-life study support: portions diverse prototypes into blind three-digit-coded containers, holds/serves them at set temperatures to a trained panel in booths, and pulls samples from stability chambers on schedule for evaluation and testing; compiles the resulting data.

General technical support in the lab: prepares reagents, standards and buffers, calibrates and maintains instruments (balances, pH meters, refractometers, titrators), washes/sterilizes glassware, receives and logs samples, stocks supplies and files documentation for the scientist.

tasks.label: Prepare or incubate slides with cell cultures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Food microbiology QC lab: technician makes stained smear slides from colonies on plates or from enrichment/broth cultures (label slide, emulsify colony in saline, smear, air-dry, heat-fix, Gram stain, rinse, blot) so an analyst can confirm morphology of Listeria, Salmonella, lactic acid bacteria, etc. Batches of 5-40 slides per shift on a standard bench near the incubators.

Wet mounts and direct microscopic counts from cell suspensions: yeast slurry viability (methylene blue) in a brewery/fermentation lab, mold spore suspensions, Breed smears of milk, or hemocytometer/counting-chamber loading of a diluted culture. Sample is a homogeneous liquid suspension in a tube; slide or counting chamber is loaded, stained if required, and passed to the microscope.

Setting up and incubating cultures: inoculating slants, plates, broth tubes or slide cultures (e.g., Riddell mold slide culture, coverslip cultures) from a food sample or stock culture, sealing/labeling, loading into 25/35/55 °C incubators for defined times, logging temperatures, and pulling them at the scheduled read time.

Mammalian/insect cell culture work in a cultivated-meat R&D or food-toxicology lab: thawing and passaging a cell line in a biosafety cabinet, seeding cells onto chamber slides or coverslips in a CO2 incubator, then fixing and staining (or live-imaging) the slides for microscopic assessment of confluence, morphology, differentiation or cytotoxicity.

Non-routine troubleshooting slides in a plant QC or pilot-plant lab: mounting whatever the investigation requires - biofilm swab material from a line, spoiled or fatty/viscous product, sediment or foreign matter from a customer complaint, a suspect starter culture - deciding the mount and stain on the spot from a variable, unstandardized matrix.

tasks.label: Mix, blend, or cultivate ingredients to make reagents or to manufacture food or beverage products.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Food QC/analytical lab: preparing reagents, buffers, standard solutions, titrants and sample diluents — weighing solids on an analytical balance, dissolving, diluting to volume in glassware, adjusting pH, labeling and logging. Pilot plant or plant floor: charging bulk and minor ingredients into mixers, blenders, kettles or tanks for a scale-up or production batch, running the blend/cook cycle to a recipe, and drawing samples to check the batch against spec.

Beverage/cultured-food fermentation work: propagating starter cultures or yeast, preparing and sterilizing growth medium, inoculating fermenters/propagation vessels, feeding, aerating and monitoring the culture through the run.

roles.description: Assist biological and medical scientists. Set up, operate, and maintain laboratory instruments and equipment, monitor experiments, collect data and samples, make observations, and calculate and record results. May analyze organic substances, such as blood, food, and drugs.

tasks.label: Conduct research, or assist in the conduct of research, including the collection of information and samples, such as blood, water, soil, plants and animals.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine bench work in a research, biotech or clinical research lab: accessioning and aliquoting specimens, pipetting reagents into plates/tubes, nucleic-acid extractions, PCR/ELISA/plate assay set-up, loading and running analyzers and centrifuges, logging results into the LIMS/notebook. Standardized protocols repeated many times per day.

Multi-step and less standardized bench work: maintaining and sampling cell or microbial cultures, media prep, gels and blots, microscopy and slide/specimen prep, dissection or tissue processing, running a new protocol for a PI, troubleshooting a failed run and maintaining instruments in a shared lab.

Collecting biological specimens from human research participants at a study clinic or draw station: venipuncture into study tubes, labeling, brief participant interaction, and immediate processing/preservation of the samples.

Vivarium/animal-facility work: handling and restraining rodents or other lab animals, serial blood draws for PK/PD studies, urine/feces/tissue collection, weighing and recording observations under IACUC protocol.

Outdoor sample and data collection at accessible, mapped sites: soil cores on a pre-set grid in agricultural or research fields, in-canopy plant/plot measurements on research plots, and water samples from lakes, coastal waters or monitored waterways, with georeferencing and labeling.

Field collection in unmanaged habitat: wading a stream or wetland for grab samples and field parameters, hiking to remote plots, small-mammal/insect trapping, netting and handling wildlife for blood/tissue and morphometrics, vegetation and habitat surveys in variable weather and terrain.

Field or greenhouse research trial: technician walks the plots or benches on a set schedule recording emergence, stand counts, plant height, phenology, and disease/pest ratings on a tablet for the research team, in variable weather and plot layouts.

Screening large numbers of small live specimens/model organisms under a scope - zebrafish larvae, C. elegans, insect colonies, embryos - for morphological abnormalities, deformities, infection or mortality in a screening or QC workflow.

On-site examination of animals or plants at a production facility (hatchery or fish farm, poultry house, dairy/livestock barn, greenhouse or nursery): walking the site to inspect stock for lesions, parasites, lameness, mortality or disease signs and sampling suspect individuals.

tasks.label: Isolate, identify and prepare specimens for examination.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Clinical, food-safety, pharma-QC or environmental microbiology bench: technician receives specimens (urine, swabs, stool, product rinses), inoculates and streaks agar plates and broths, incubates, picks isolated colonies for purity subculture, makes Gram-stain smears, and prepares picked colonies for identification (MALDI-TOF or biochemical panel) and susceptibility setup. Indoor lab, standard labware, specimens of mixed container types.

Molecular sample preparation: technician takes blood, swab, tissue lysate, plant or cultured-cell material, performs nucleic acid or protein extraction and purification (spin column or magnetic bead), quantifies, normalizes, and lays out plates for PCR/qPCR or NGS library preparation so the sample can be run and the organism/target identified. Indoor lab, tubes and 96-well plates.

Cell and tissue culture: technician thaws or isolates cells (cell lines, primary cells, iPSC, organoids), feeds and passages them in a biosafety cabinet, checks morphology and confluence by microscope, counts cells, and prepares suspensions, aliquots, chamber slides or assay plates for downstream examination. Indoor lab with hoods and incubators, sterile technique required.

Histology/cytology slide preparation: fixed tissue already trimmed into cassettes is processed, embedded in paraffin, sectioned on a microtome, floated and mounted on slides, stained (H&E or special/IHC) and coverslipped so a pathologist or researcher can examine it; also preparation of stained blood or cytology smears. Indoor histology lab with processors, embedders, microtomes, stainers.

Whole-organism work in a lab/necropsy room: technician dissects animals (rodents, fish, insects) or plants to isolate specific organs, tissues or structures, trims and preserves them (fixative, freezing, RNAlater) and labels them for downstream examination. Deformable, variable-anatomy specimens, scalpel and forceps work under a hood or dissecting scope.

Bulk field-collected sample workup: a mixed sample of small invertebrates (malaise trap catch, benthic sample, plankton) or seeds/plant material is sorted specimen by specimen under a stereo microscope, each specimen identified to family/morphotype, imaged or measured, and transferred into vials or 96-well plates for barcoding or curation. Indoor lab bench.

tasks.label: Clean, maintain and prepare supplies and work areas.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine decontamination of work surfaces in a research/clinical lab: spraying and wiping bench tops, biosafety cabinet interiors, shared instrument surfaces and fume hood decks with 70% ethanol or dilute bleach before and after work, and wiping up small spills. Benches are cluttered with instruments, tube racks, cables, notebooks and samples that must be moved and replaced.

Washing and sterilizing labware and supplies: collecting dirty glassware, bottles, tubs, plastic caging and instrument parts, running them through a glassware washer or cage/tunnel washer, loading and unloading the autoclave, drying, and putting the clean, sterile items back into storage.

Preparing and restocking consumables: receiving and unpacking supply deliveries, putting stock away, checking inventory and expiry, refilling pipette-tip racks, tube racks, gloves and wash bottles, and staging labware, plates and reagents at the bench or instrument for the day's runs.

Preparing sterile media, buffers and solutions in advance of experiments: weighing and dissolving powders, sterilizing/autoclaving media, pouring agar plates, aliquoting buffers into bottles/tubes, labeling and storing them at the correct temperature.

Routine cleaning and upkeep of installed equipment: wiping out and decontaminating CO2 incubators and water baths, cleaning centrifuge rotors and chambers, defrosting freezers, changing filters and tubing, refilling reservoirs, checking and topping up gas/liquid supplies, and logging maintenance.

Lab waste handling and general tidying: emptying and re-lining biohazard and general waste bins, sealing and labeling autoclave/sharps waste, segregating chemical waste, hauling waste and soiled-linen carts to the collection point, and mopping or tidying the work area at end of day.

Field equipment work at outdoor sites: transporting and deploying multiparameter sondes, data loggers, automated samplers, weather stations, traps and GPS units; calibrating in the field, clearing biofouling/debris, swapping batteries and desiccant, retrieving data, and repairing damage in variable weather and terrain.

tasks.label: Conduct standardized biological, microbiological or biochemical tests and laboratory analyses to evaluate the quantity or quality of physical or chemical substances in food or other products.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Food/beverage QC or contract testing lab: routine culture-based microbiology on product samples (aerobic plate count, coliform/E. coli, yeast & mold). Technician weighs 25 g into a blender bag, makes serial dilutions, pours/spreads agar plates or Petrifilm, incubates, counts colonies, reports CFU/g to LIMS under ISO/BAM/AOAC methods; dozens of samples per shift.

Pathogen presence/absence testing on food or environmental samples: 25 g portion enriched overnight in broth, aliquot loaded to an automated immunoassay or PCR platform, negatives released, presumptive positives streaked to selective agar and confirmed; results reported in 24-48 h in an accredited lab.

Instrumental chemical/biochemical analysis of food or other products: homogenize and weigh sample, solvent extraction or QuEChERS cleanup, filter into autosampler vials, run HPLC/GC-MS/ICP-MS, verify QC standards and calibration, integrate peaks and report concentrations of pesticide residues, mycotoxins, vitamins, additives or metals.

Pharma/biotech/consumer-product QC or research-support lab: plate-based biochemical and bioassay testing (ELISA, protein quantification, enzyme activity, endotoxin/LAL, cell-based potency). Serial dilutions and reagent additions into 96-well plates, timed incubations and washes, plate reading, standard-curve fitting, acceptance-criteria check.

Routine physicochemical quality checks on liquid or semi-liquid products (pH, titratable acidity, salt or chloride titration, Brix, moisture, viscosity of a beverage/sauce/dairy sample): pour subsample into beaker/cup, run meter or autotitrator, compare to specification and log result.

Sample-prep-heavy tests on irregular raw or packaged items: aseptically opening varied retail packaging, excising a representative 25 g portion from a raw poultry carcass, whole produce or a composite mixed meal, judging what constitutes a representative subsample, then homogenizing and testing.

tasks.label: Participate in the research, development, or manufacturing of medicinal and pharmaceutical preparations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Discovery/preclinical R&D bench assay in a pharma or biotech screening lab: prepare compound dilution series and reagents, dispense cells or biochemical mixes into 96/384-well plates, incubate, add detection reagents, read plates, and log data for a drug-candidate screen or dose-response follow-up. Standard labware, established written protocols, repeated daily.

Cell culture and biologics/cell-therapy development work: maintain and expand mammalian cell lines or donor primary cells in biosafety cabinets and incubators (media exchange, passaging, viability counts, cryovial banking), and sample small-scale bioreactors supporting a drug-development program. Aseptic technique, multi-week campaigns.

GMP QC/analytical testing of drug substance and drug product in a controlled QC lab: weigh and dissolve samples, prepare standards, run potency/HPLC, dissolution, bioburden/sterility and environmental-monitoring plate testing, and record results against specification for release or stability studies.

Manufacturing/production support in a cleanroom or bioprocess suite: prepare media and buffers, set up and in-process sample bioreactors or purification steps, and support aseptic fill-finish or cell-therapy batch manufacture (handling nested vials, bags, tubing) under gowning and SOPs.

Non-routine bench work in R&D: set up a novel or modified preparation - a new formulation trial, a custom apparatus or glassware rig, a one-off scale-up, or troubleshooting a failed/anomalous run - where protocol, labware and bench layout change each time and the technician improvises within the lab as found.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench prep support in an academic or industry research lab: pulling stocks from shelves/fridges, weighing and dissolving powders, making buffers, media and reagent master mixes, adjusting pH, autoclaving, aliquoting, labeling and staging plates/tubes so a scientist's experiment can run that day. Protocols change frequently between projects.

Executing routine assays and sample processing on scientists' behalf: nucleic acid extraction, PCR/qPCR setup, ELISA and plate assays, gels, cell culture passaging, microscopy/plate reading; then recording, QC-ing and returning the data. Samples arrive in batches with variable labware in a shared lab.

Equipment and facility support: setting up and calibrating instruments (balances, pipettes, centrifuges, spectrophotometers, HPLC, sequencers), preventive maintenance, diagnosing and fixing failures mid-run, sterilizing/decontaminating, glassware and hazardous waste handling, restocking consumables and keeping safety/compliance records for the lab's scientists.

Field support for environmental, resource-management or agricultural scientists: traveling to plots, streams, forests or coastal sites; collecting georeferenced soil, water or plant samples; taking in-situ measurements; bagging, labeling, preserving and transporting samples back to the lab, in whatever weather and terrain the site presents.

Greenhouse, growth-chamber or animal-facility support for researchers: sowing/transplanting, watering and weighing pots, tagging plots, taking growth and phenotype measurements on schedule, maintaining environmental conditions and logging the data for the responsible scientist.

Direct hands-on assistance to scientists, postdocs and students: demonstrating a technique at the bench, training a new user on an instrument, walking through a failed protocol with them and advising on fixes and on ordering the right supplies.
